problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -3 \\ 15 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +52 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=4\pm 6\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =4-6\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=4-6\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4-6\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4-6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+6\text{i} & -3 \\ 15 & -3+6\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3+6\text{i}){x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 15{x}_{1}+(-3+6\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(1+2\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+2\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$
